title: Review of lab 1's ad5-evolve: Weak. The fastest catalyst allele does rise to most droplets on fresh seeds 11-12 while an equal-rate neutral twin keeps its ancestor majority. But generations reach only 2, and part of the rise is mutation converting living droplets, not births
summary: labkit re-runs of the lab 1 world (unchanged) on fresh seeds 11 and 12 (t=20000) give 5-6 persistent splits, max generation 2 and 0 merges. Per-allele droplet counts (alleles.py on the render frames): the fastest allele a3 (k=0.16) goes from 0 to 7 and 10 droplets and the ancestor a0 (k=0.10, sterile) falls from 6-7 to 2. In a neutral twin with all four rates equal at 0.13 (same seeds, same mutation and dilution machinery), the ancestor allele stays the majority (6 and 5 droplets at the end, peak 12 and 9) and the mutant alleles reach only 1-3 droplets each. So the bias toward a3 comes from its rate, not from the mutation scheme. a3 gains up to 10 droplets from only 5-6 persistent splits in the whole run, so several a3 droplets arose by a mutation patch taking over a living droplet (sheet.png seed 12: a lavender droplet turns white at t~13100). That is conversion, which RUBRIC L7 does not count as selection. Deaths happen only through random dilution disks.

observations.H: alleles_c27.png: a3 rises to 7/10 droplets in the world and stays at 3/3 in the equal-rate neutral twin, where the ancestor allele keeps 6/5

verdicts.limitation: My neutral twin sets every rate to 0.13, so the ancestor can divide; the ancestor-matched neutral at 0.10 is sterile (lab 1), which makes it trivial. This twin tests direction, not the ancestor's baseline. The new alleles enter by an imposed patch transplant inside living droplets, and part of the a3 rise is such conversions; I did not count conversions per mutation event. Two seeds only.
